title: AI-Enabled Early Prediction of Lassa Fever: A Clinical Decision Support System for Endemic Settings

analysis.research_question_and_background: Lassa fever remains a major public health challenge in West Africa, where early clinical symptoms frequently overlap with other febrile illnesses and laboratory confirmation may be delayed.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study developed and evaluated an AI-enabled Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) to support early triage of suspected Lassa fever cases using a retrospective clinical surveillance dataset from Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital, Nigeria, spanning 2015 to 2025, one of the largest longitudinal clinical surveillance datasets for Lassa fever. The final cohort included 31,277 patient encounters, with 3,359 laboratory-confirmed cases (10.7% prevalence).
analysis.methods: Four supervised models (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, and XGBoost) were evaluated using temporal validation, with recent years reserved for independent testing. The model was deployed as a lightweight web-based CDSS with integrated feature-level explanations, which demonstrated the feasibility of the real-time AI-assisted triage using routine clinical surveillance data in endemic settings.
analysis.main_results: On the temporal test set, the selected XGBoost model achieved ROC-AUC of 0.664, AUPRC of 0.137, and Brier score of 0.057. Predicted probabilities were stratified into Low (≤0.155), Medium (0.155–0.310), and High (>0.310) risk categories, with observed positivity rates increasing across bands (3.9%, 8.7%, and 16.1%, respectively).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our findings highlight the potential of AI-driven tools to support early decision-making and optimise resource allocation for Lassa fever control.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying AI tools in endemic settings to improve early triage and resource allocation for Lassa fever, which can inform the development of similar systems for other arenavirus infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used a retrospective dataset and did not include prospective validation, which may limit the generalisability of the model. The evidence strength is moderate due to the reliance on historical data and the absence of direct clinical outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to address the challenge of early Lassa fever diagnosis in West Africa, where symptoms often overlap with other febrile illnesses and laboratory confirmation is delayed. A Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) was developed and evaluated using a large longitudinal dataset from Nigeria. The XGBoost model demonstrated moderate performance with ROC-AUC of 0.664 and AUPRC of 0.137. Predicted risk categories showed increasing positivity rates with higher risk scores. The study highlights the potential of AI tools to aid in early decision-making and resource allocation for Lassa fever control. However, the use of retrospective data and lack of prospective validation limit the generalisability of the findings.

title: Reported case fatality as a target and trial metric in endemic zoonoses: a framework and ecological analysis of Lassa fever surveillance in Nigeria, 2017-2026

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address concerns about the rising reported Lassa fever case fatality ratio (CFR) in Nigeria, 2025-2026, and to determine whether this increase reflected changes in clinical care or surveillance practices.
analysis.study_design_and_population: An ecological study was conducted using weekly state-level counts from 474 Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention situation reports spanning 2017-2026, focusing on Lassa fever surveillance in Nigeria.
analysis.methods: Weekly incident and cumulative published totals were compared post hoc, and a pre-specified plan was used to compare years at phase-matched points, decompose year-on-year CFR changes into within-state and between-state components, and calculate tipping-point ascertainment shifts.
analysis.main_results: On weekly incident counts, 2026 did not differ from 2025 at the phase-matched midpoint (+0.3 percentage points, 95% CI -5.0 to 7.6); within-state (-1.1, 95% CI -4.7 to 3.0) and between-state (+0.5, -2.0 to 2.9) components spanned zero. The published cumulative CFR was 5.4 to 6.2 percentage points higher due to 70 deaths added retrospectively by week 36 outside weekly reports.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The 2026 CFR rise was attributed to deaths added to cumulative totals outside the weekly counts, and the study concluded that published data cannot attribute this to changes in clinical care. It introduced a framework for analyzing reported CFR changes in zoonoses with recurrent spillover.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for transparency in surveillance data to accurately interpret CFR changes in endemic zoonoses, which is critical for planning vaccine trials and tracking progress towards national CFR targets.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is limited by the fact that data on testing volumes, deaths added late, and post-mortem sampling are collected but not published, which affects the ability to fully assess the validity of CFR changes. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the reported case fatality ratio (CFR) of Lassa fever in Nigeria from 2017 to 2026, addressing concerns about its rise from 18.9% in 2025 to 25.0% in 2026. It highlights the importance of distinguishing between changes in CFR due to surveillance practices and actual clinical outcomes. The ecological analysis extracted weekly state-level counts from Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention reports and decomposed CFR changes into within-state and between-state components. The results showed that the 2026 CFR increase was not evident in weekly incident counts but was attributed to retrospective additions of deaths to cumulative totals. The study emphasizes that without transparency in surveillance data, CFR changes cannot be reliably interpreted as reflecting clinical outcomes. It introduces a framework for analyzing CFR changes in zoonoses with recurrent spillover, which is essential for planning vaccine trials and tracking public health progress. However, the study's evidence is limited by the lack of published data on testing volumes and late death reporting, which affects the interpretation of CFR trends.

title: MerTK mediates dexamethasone-induced suppression of antiviral CD8+ T cell immunity and exacerbates chronic LCMV infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the impact of dexamethasone on antiviral CD8+ T cell immunity during chronic LCMV infection and to understand the mechanisms underlying its immunosuppressive effects. The background highlights the complex and often contradictory effects of glucocorticoids on antiviral immunity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used wild-type (Mertk +/+) and MerTK-deficient (Mertk –/–) mice infected with the LCMV Docile strain. Animals were randomly assigned to receive either PBS or dexamethasone (2.5mg/kg) intraperitoneally every 48 hours. Blood, spleen, and liver samples were collected on day 8 post-infection for analysis.
